analysis.one_liner: Bans agencies from buying Americans' location and personal data from brokers without a court order.
analysis.headline: The bill drew six bipartisan cosponsors but never got a committee vote, dying in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal, state, and local law enforcement and intelligence agencies can currently buy Americans' location, browsing, and communications records from data brokers without a warrant. This bill would make that illegal, requiring agencies to get a court order under the same strict standards that apply to phone and internet companies. It would also close a path around surveillance law by making the warrant process of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act the only legal route for foreign-intelligence collection of Americans' location and browsing history from U.S. companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans. The bill would restore warrant protection to personal data that people effectively give up every day — phone location, web browsing, app activity — when that data ends up with brokers who sell it to government agencies. People whose records were wrongly purchased would gain a remedy, since data bought in violation could not be used against them in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans whose personal data is sold

how_it_helps.text: Bars law enforcement agencies and intelligence agencies from obtaining records about people in the U.S. from third parties in exchange for anything of value, including access, service, and licensing fees, and applies even when the data passed through multiple hands.

Requires a court order before a third party can be forced to hand over such records, with courts applying the most stringent standard under federal statute or the Constitution that would apply to a comparable demand on a phone or internet provider.

Prohibits data bought or shared in violation of the ban from being used as evidence in any U.S. court or proceeding, and requires the Attorney General to adopt procedures to minimize and destroy such improperly acquired information.

Makes the warrant process of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act the exclusive legal route for foreign-intelligence collection of Americans' location information, web browsing history, and internet search history from U.S. companies, closing side channels around FISA.

Extends the existing ban on communications providers divulging call contents and subscriber records to 'intermediary service providers' — companies that deliver, store, or process communications behind the scenes for phone and internet services.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and ad-tech companies that sell Americans' location and personal data would lose a major customer: government agencies. Police and intelligence agencies would lose a shortcut and have to get court orders instead. Telecommunications and internet companies that sell subscriber data or assist agencies without court orders would face new limits and narrower legal immunity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and data-selling tech firms

drawbacks.text: The bill makes evidence obtained in violation unusable in any proceeding, a strong remedy that in a real case could let someone who committed a serious crime go free because of how the evidence was gathered.

The ban is absolute and applies even where commercially available data has helped agencies locate missing people, trafficking victims, or fugitives quickly; agencies would have to route those urgent cases through court orders or narrow emergency exceptions instead.

It restricts only government purchases. Data brokers would still be free to sell the same Americans' location and personal data to any private buyer, so the underlying market in personal data would continue largely untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: warrant protection for data that today can be bought about nearly anyone without a judge ever seeing a request. The costs are manageable, because the bill does not eliminate access — agencies can still obtain records through court orders under the strictest applicable standard, and emergency legal channels remain for urgent interceptions. The biggest honest criticism is that it disciplines only the government side of the data-broker market while leaving the market itself intact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late July 2023 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, and no committee ever considered it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act on July 27, 2023.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, which was the last action ever taken on it.
Six senators cosponsored the bill — two Republicans and four Democrats — giving it support from both parties.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the Judiciary Committee holding a markup or the Senate ever voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers came out ahead: they keep selling Americans' location and personal data to law enforcement and intelligence agencies, and agencies keep buying it without a warrant. The companies collecting and reselling the data keep the revenue channel, and Americans remain without the warrant protection the bill would have restored.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and their government customers

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines — a Democratic sponsor joined by 2 of 49 Senate Republicans and 4 of 48 Senate Democrats — but no votes were ever recorded, so the final split was never tested.

industries.note: Data brokers sell Americans' location and personal records, often scraped or bought from apps and telecoms, to law enforcement and intelligence agencies that thereby avoid needing a warrant. The bill cuts off that government revenue channel, so the industry's interest runs directly against the privacy of ordinary people.

The bill extends the ban on divulging call contents and subscriber records to intermediary companies that process communications behind the scenes, and narrows the civil immunity of companies assisting the government without a court order. That closes revenue and cooperation channels these firms currently use with agencies.

Companies feeding location and behavioral data into the broker market would face the bill's definitions of illegitimately obtained information — data gathered by deceiving users, breaking contracts, or violating privacy policies could not be sold to the government. But the bill does not regulate their sales to private buyers, so their core business would continue.
